verses.text: David was told, “Behold, the Philistines are fighting against Keilah, and are robbing the threshing floors.”
Therefore David inquired of Yahweh, saying, “Shall I go and strike these Philistines?” Yahweh said to David, “Go strike the Philistines, and save Keilah.”
David’s men said to him, “Behold, we are afraid here in Judah. How much more then if we go to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines?”
Then David inquired of Yahweh yet again. Yahweh answered him, and said, “Arise, go down to Keilah; for I will deliver the Philistines into your hand.”
David and his men went to Keilah, and fought with the Philistines, and brought away their livestock, and killed them with a great slaughter. So David saved the inhabitants of Keilah.
When Abiathar the son of Ahimelech fled to David to Keilah, he came down with an ephod in his hand.
Saul was told that David had come to Keilah. Saul said, “God has delivered him into my hand; for he is shut in by entering into a town that has gates and bars.”
Saul summoned all the people to war, to go down to Keilah, to besiege David and his men.
David knew that Saul was devising mischief against him; and he said to Abiathar the priest, “Bring the ephod here.”
Then David said, “O Yahweh, the God of Israel, your servant has surely heard that Saul seeks to come to Keilah, to destroy the city for my sake.
Will the men of Keilah deliver me up into his hand? Will Saul come down, as your servant has heard? Yahweh, the God of Israel, I beg you, tell your servant.” Yahweh said, “He will come down.”
Then David said, “Will the men of Keilah deliver me and my men into the hand of Saul?” Yahweh said, “They will deliver you up.”
Then David and his men, who were about six hundred, arose and departed out of Keilah, and went wherever they could go. Saul was told that David was escaped from Keilah; and he gave up going there.
David stayed in the wilderness in the strongholds, and remained in the hill country in the wilderness of Ziph. Saul sought him every day, but God didn’t deliver him into his hand.
David saw that Saul had come out to seek his life. David was in the wilderness of Ziph in the wood.
Jonathan, Saul’s son, arose, and went to David into the woods, and strengthened his hand in God.
He said to him, “Don’t be afraid; for the hand of Saul my father won’t find you; and you will be king over Israel, and I will be next to you; and Saul my father knows that also.”
They both made a covenant before Yahweh. Then David stayed in the woods, and Jonathan went to his house.
Then the Ziphites came up to Saul to Gibeah, saying, “Doesn’t David hide himself with us in the strongholds in the woods, in the hill of Hachilah, which is on the south of the desert?
Now therefore, O king, come down. According to all the desire of your soul to come down; and our part will be to deliver him up into the king’s hand.”
Saul said, “You are blessed by Yahweh; for you have had compassion on me.
Please go make yet more sure, and know and see his place where his haunt is, and who has seen him there; for I have been told that he deals very crafty.

See therefore, and take knowledge of all the lurking places where he hides himself, and come again to me with certainty, and I will go with you. It shall happen, if he is in the land, that I will search him out among all the thousands of Judah.”
They arose, and went to Ziph before Saul: but David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the Arabah on the south of the desert.
Saul and his men went to seek him. When David was told, he went down to the rock, and stayed in the wilderness of Maon. When Saul heard that, he pursued David in the wilderness of Maon.

Saul went on this side of the mountain, and David and his men on that side of the mountain; and David hurried to get away for fear of Saul; for Saul and his men surrounded David and his men to take them.
But a messenger came to Saul, saying, “Hurry and come; for the Philistines have made a raid on the land!”
So Saul returned from pursuing David, and went against the Philistines. Therefore they called that place Sela Hammahlekoth.
David went up from there, and lived in the strongholds of En Gedi.

footnotes.content: The news came: raiders at Keilah, taking the harvest that meant survival. David heard the need and turned to the Lord before turning to arms. That instinct—to ask first, to seek the Father's mind before the fight—is the mark of a heart that knows who is truly in charge.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When David asked, the answer came clear: Go. Strike. Save. The Lord gave him both the command and the assurance. That is how the Father leads—not by riddles or silence, but by direct word to a son who listens. David's courage came not from his strength, but from having heard his Father speak.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His men were afraid. Six hundred men, trained warriors, and still the thought of Keilah's gates felt like a trap. Fear speaks loudly to the crowd, but David had learned a quieter voice—the voice that asked the Lord again and again. Fear and faith can both speak at once; which one will you hear?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David asked a second time, and the Lord answered again. Not once, but twice—the Father's patience with our doubt is deeper than we can measure. The answer stayed the same: Arise. Go down. I will deliver. When doubt rises in us, a word from the Lord settles everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Keilah lies near the Philistine lands, a town in constant shadow of raid. That David brought livestock back—not just soldiers—meant the people could eat, rebuild. When a man walks in the Lord's will, mercy flows not just to the grateful, but even to those who will later betray him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abiathar came with the ephod—the priestly instrument for hearing God's voice. Ahimelech's son carried the means of seeking the Lord. He had fled to David because David's men needed more than swords; they needed a priest. The Lord sends us the helpers we do not yet know we need.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul saw a locked cage: David in a walled town with bars. Saul thought the Lord had delivered David to him. But Saul did not know what David knew—that the Lord was with David, not against him. Desperation makes us imagine traps the Lord has already sprung open.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul called all Israel to war—a king marshaling a nation against one man on the run. The weight and machinery of earthly power moved to crush David. Yet David had something Saul forgot he'd thrown away: the heart of a man who sought the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David knew. Not by spy or rumor, but by discernment—he saw Saul's heart turning again to mischief. Then he asked for the ephod. When danger tightens around us, wisdom is to seek the Lord's counsel, not to hide or run blind into the night.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David spoke the fear openly: *Saul seeks to come here and destroy this city for my sake.* He did not hide from the weight of it. He named the danger and brought it before the Lord with a servant's honest voice. The Father draws near to a heart that tells Him the truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two questions: Will the men deliver me? Will Saul come down? Both answered in order—Yes, and Yes. The Lord did not spare David the hard news. Sometimes love means telling us what we do not wish to hear. The gift is knowing, not ignorance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The men of Keilah would turn David over to buy their own peace. People are people—grateful one day, practical the next. David did not rage at this; he accepted what the Lord had told him and moved. Expectation of betrayal is the guard that keeps us from despair.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Six hundred men arose and left. That is a company, not a rabble—strong enough to move through the wilderness, small enough to vanish. David took his people and went *wherever they could go*—a picture of the faithful on the run, guided by the Lord step by uncertain step.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wilderness strongholds. Ziph's hills. Saul searched every day, but God did not deliver David. The Lord was a shield that no pursuit could pierce. In the hardest seasons of our faith, we learn that the Father's protection is not always loud or visible—sometimes it is simply: *He was not found.*
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David saw that Saul had come out to seek his life—a man hunted in his own land, hiding in the woods. The knowledge of danger weighed on him. But he remained in the wilderness of Ziph, waiting on the Lord. To stand when you could run takes a different kind of courage.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan came to the woods where David hid, and strengthened his hand in God. In that moment, Saul's own son became the Lord's messenger—a reminder that kinship with the Father can be closer than kinship with blood. Sometimes He sends us the friend we did not expect to find us there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan named the truth: *You will be king over Israel, and I will be next to you, and Saul my father knows that also.* He had seen the Lord's hand on David and accepted it, even though it meant surrender of his own throne. That is the friendship the Lord honors—one that loves rightly by letting go.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They made a covenant before the Lord in those woods. No witnesses but the trees and heaven. Then Jonathan went home, and David stayed hidden. True covenant does not require an audience—it holds between the friends and their Father, sealed in the wilderness where only God sees.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Ziphites knew the strongholds—Hachilah lay south of the desert, a place where a fugitive might hide. They knew the land the way neighbours know it, and they offered that knowledge to the king for his reward. Geography becomes a weapon when a man is hunting another man.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They promised delivery—their part would be to hand David over. Such small words for such a betrayal. A price is named, a favour is promised, and a man becomes merchandise. The Ziphites show us how easily the comfortable will trade another's life for the king's smile.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul blessed them: *You are blessed by Yahweh.* A king's gratitude for betrayal. He meant it—in that moment, Saul truly believed the Ziphites were the Lord's instruments. Yet the Lord's heart rested with David in the woods, not with Saul on his throne.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Make sure, know, see—Saul wanted certainty before he moved. He had heard David was crafty, a man who moved like shadow. A king can command kingdoms, but he cannot command sight into hidden places. Only the Lord sees where a man is hiding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul promised to search all the thousands of Judah. The machinery of a nation turned to find one man. Yet Saul did not know that the search was already decided—by a messenger who would come, by a Philistine raid that would call him away, by the Lord's quiet will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Maon lay in the Arabah, south of the desert—another wilderness stronghold where a company could move unseen. The Ziphites went to meet Saul, but David and his men had already slipped away, reading the land like a man reads the face of a friend.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the word came to David, he moved again—to rock, to stronghold, to safety. Saul heard, pursued, but found himself always one step behind. The hunter became the hunted. When a man walks with the Lord, the machinery of the world cannot keep its grip on him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mountain on either side—Saul on one slope, David on the other, with the valley between them. Saul's men encircled, drawing close. David hurried to escape. We see in that moment the narrowing—the walls closing in, the king's hand almost upon him. Yet the Father had already arranged what no man could arrange.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A messenger came with one word: Hurry. The Philistines were raiding again. In that moment, Saul's pursuit of David stopped. Not because David was stronger, but because the Lord moved in Saul's own affairs to pull him away. We cannot see the Lord's hand, yet it moves through all things.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sela Hammahlekoth—*the Rock of Divisions*, or *the Rock of Escape*. The place where the kingdom was divided, where Saul turned back and David slipped free, became a name on the map. The Lord marks the places where His deliverance happens.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in that final movement: David went up from there to En Gedi, the spring by the Dead Sea where life flourishes in harsh land. When the Father leads us through the narrow places, He leads us to springs—not because we deserved them, but because He is merciful. As of 2026-10, I am grateful still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
